section.title: Freedom for Slaves Betrayed
section.sectionRationale: As Babylon's army presses the siege, Zedekiah leads Jerusalem in a covenant to free every Hebrew slave, a genuine act of repentance obeying the law of release. But once the immediate danger eases, the same officials seize back the men and women they had freed, and God answers their broken covenant with a chilling judgment: the freedom they refused their neighbors, He will proclaim for them instead, freedom to fall by sword, famine, and plague.
section.thesis: A covenant of freedom made before God and then reversed for convenience is not a small betrayal but a direct assault on the character of the God who Himself freed Israel from slavery in Egypt, and God will not let such treachery stand, so those who profaned His name by re-enslaving their brothers will find He proclaims a very different freedom over them.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: God's word to Zedekiah that Jerusalem will fall but he himself will die in peace; the covenant to free every Hebrew slave, sincerely made and then treacherously broken; God's rebuke recalling the covenant He made at the exodus and the sabbatical release law it echoed; and the judgment, freedom to sword, famine, and plague, for those who profaned His name.

units.label: Word to Zedekiah: the city will fall, but he will die in peace

verses.text: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, all his army, all the earthly kingdoms under his control, and all the other nations were fighting against Jerusalem and all its surrounding cities.

The LORD, the God of Israel, told Jeremiah to go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah and tell him that this is what the LORD says: “Behold, I am about to deliver this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will burn it down.

And you yourself will not escape his grasp, but will surely be captured and delivered into his hand. You will see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face; and you will go to Babylon.
Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah. This is what the LORD says concerning you: You will not die by the sword;

you will die in peace. As spices were burned for your fathers, the former kings who preceded you, so people will burn spices for you and lament, ‘Alas, O master!’ For I Myself have spoken this word, declares the LORD.”
In Jerusalem, then, Jeremiah the prophet relayed all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah
as the army of the king of Babylon was fighting against Jerusalem and the remaining cities of Judah, against Lachish and Azekah. For these were the only fortified cities remaining in Judah.

units.label: A covenant to free the slaves

verses.text: After King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to proclaim {{deror|liberty}}, the word came to Jeremiah from the LORD
that each man should free his Hebrew slaves, both male and female, and no one should hold his fellow Jew in bondage.

So all the officials and all the people who entered into this covenant agreed that they would free their menservants and maidservants and no longer hold them in bondage. They obeyed and released them,
but later they changed their minds and took back the menservants and maidservants they had freed, and they forced them to become slaves again.

units.label: God's rebuke: broken covenant, contrasted with Egypt

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,
“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I made a covenant with your forefathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, saying:

Every seventh year, each of you must free his Hebrew brother who has sold himself to you. He may serve you six years, but then you must let him go free. But your fathers did not listen or incline their ear.
Recently you repented and did what pleased Me; each of you proclaimed freedom for his neighbor. You made a covenant before Me in the house that bears My Name.

But now you have changed your minds and profaned My name. Each of you has taken back the menservants and maidservants whom you had set at liberty to go wherever they wanted, and you have again forced them to be your slaves.

units.label: Judgment: freedom to sword, famine, and plague

verses.text: Therefore this is what the LORD says: You have not obeyed Me; you have not proclaimed freedom, each man for his brother and for his neighbor. So now I proclaim {{deror|freedom}} for you, declares the LORD, freedom to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine! I will make you a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.

And those who have transgressed My covenant and have not fulfilled the terms of the covenant they made before Me, I will treat like the calf they {{karatBerit|cut}} in two in order to pass between its pieces.
The officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the court officials, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the pieces of the calf,
I will deliver into the hands of their enemies who seek their lives. Their corpses will become food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth.
And I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials into the hands of their enemies who seek their lives, to the army of the king of Babylon that had withdrawn from you.

Behold, I am going to give the command, declares the LORD, and I will bring them back to this city. They will fight against it, capture it, and burn it down. And I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant.”

deror.gloss: Liberty, release, a free flight. The same word that names the Year of Jubilee, Leviticus 25:10, and the release Isaiah promises the captives, Isaiah 61:1, later read by Jesus of Himself, Luke 4:18. Here the officials proclaim deror to their slaves and then take it back, so God proclaims a very different deror over them instead.

karatBerit.gloss: Literally to cut a covenant. Ancient covenant ceremonies involved cutting an animal in two and walking between the pieces, symbolizing the fate of anyone who broke the sworn terms. Those who broke this covenant will themselves be treated like the calf they cut.

basic.context: With Babylon's army at the gates, Zedekiah leads Jerusalem in a covenant to free every Hebrew slave, obeying a law from Sinai that had long been ignored. But once circumstances shifted, the same officials broke their word and re-enslaved the very people they had freed, provoking a severe judgment for profaning God's name.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage takes a real, specific covenant broken under real historical pressure and shows how seriously God takes covenant faithfulness, especially toward the vulnerable. The wordplay is deliberate: because they refused to proclaim deror, freedom, for their slaves, God proclaims a very different deror over them, freedom to die by sword, famine, and plague.
basic.originalLanguages: The officials proclaim deror, liberty, for their slaves, the same word used of the Year of Jubilee and later of the release Christ announces in Luke 4:18. When they break the covenant, God says He will treat them like the calf they karatBerit, cut, in the ancient ritual that made covenant breaking a matter of life and death.
basic.typology: The proclamation of deror, liberty, that Judah's officials made and broke anticipates the true and lasting deror Christ proclaims in Luke 4:18-19, quoting Isaiah 61:1, liberty to the captives that He never revokes. The broken covenant ritual of the cut calf anticipates the seriousness of covenant breaking that Christ's own covenant, sealed in His blood rather than an animal's, was designed to answer permanently.
basic.christ: Where Judah's leaders proclaimed liberty and then took it back, Christ proclaims liberty to the captives and never withdraws it, Luke 4:18-19. His own blood seals a covenant that cannot be broken from His side, unlike the covenant of the cut calf that Judah's officials violated so quickly after making it.
basic.god: God is the original liberator, He brought Israel out of the house of slavery in Egypt, and He takes personal offense when His people re-enslave those they had freed in His name. He is also patient with genuine, if short-lived, repentance, noting that the people had recently done what pleased Him before reversing course, yet He does not let the reversal go unanswered.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 25:10 establishes deror, liberty, at the Year of Jubilee as a defining mark of God's covenant people. Isaiah 61:1 promises deror to captives, later read by Jesus of Himself in Luke 4:18-19. Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 give the sabbatical release law Judah's officials had ignored for generations. Genesis 15:9-17 shows the same covenant-cutting ceremony God now turns into a judgment.
basic.oneStory: Judah's leaders proclaimed freedom and then betrayed it, provoking God's judgment because true covenant faithfulness cannot be reversed at convenience. That failure highlights, by contrast, the liberty Christ proclaims and never revokes, the true and lasting release the sabbatical law and this broken covenant could only foreshadow and, in their failure, point toward.

context.literary:
Chapter 34 is a diptych joined by an ordinary little word. The first panel, verses 1 to 7, is a private word of the LORD to the king. The second, verses 8 to 22, is a public story about the people, and its opening clause 'After King Zedekiah had made a covenant' links them. Both panels are set inside the same war, and verse 7 stands as the bridge between them: the Babylonian army is fighting against Jerusalem and the only two fortified cities left in Judah, Lachish and Azekah. The reader is meant to feel the walls closing.

The second panel is carefully built as a three step lawsuit. Verses 8 to 11 narrate the facts: the covenant to proclaim freedom, the obedience, and the reversal. Verses 12 to 16 are the charge, and in it the LORD takes the stand as the one who made the original law, quoting his own command of the exodus and the seventh year. Verses 17 to 22 are the sentence, and the sentence is built from the crime. The people refused to proclaim freedom, so the LORD proclaims 'freedom' for them in verse 17, and the word is turned into a threat. The covenant ritual is turned too. The people had walked between the halves of a calf to bind themselves, and the LORD says he will give them to be like the calf, verses 18 to 20. Throughout the chapter the punishment is poetic justice, each thing done to a neighbour done back by God to the doers.

The chapter also shows a contrast of two kings. Verses 4 and 5 are tender. The LORD promises Zedekiah an honoured death and a funeral with spices, in language very different from the sentence on Jehoiakim in Jeremiah 22:18 to 19. Then the chapter ends with the same king handed over, verse 21. The opening promise and the closing threat do not contradict each other. They are the two possible futures that a king who still has a choice faces, and the chapter is preparing the reader for the scenes of choice in Jeremiah 37 and 38.
context.historical:
The siege of Jerusalem had begun in Zedekiah's ninth year, 2 Kings 25:1, and it was lifted briefly when an Egyptian force marched out. Jeremiah 37:5 reports that the Chaldeans 'withdrew from Jerusalem' when they heard of Pharaoh's army. Verse 21 of our chapter says the same, calling the Babylonian army the one 'that had withdrawn from you'. The reversal in verse 11 therefore fits a moment of relief. The pressure came off, and the people who had been frightened into obedience turned back to their convenience. Ezekiel 17:15 adds that Zedekiah had sought Egypt's help against Babylon, so the king's own policy was bound up with that hope.

The law the officials broke was an old one. Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 to 15 required that a Hebrew who had sold himself into service go free in the seventh year, and Deuteronomy 15 says he must be sent off with provisions and that the reason is memory, 'Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt'. Leviticus 25:39 to 42 adds that a countryman who becomes destitute must not be forced into slave labour and is to be released with his children at the Jubilee. The prophet's accusation in verse 14, 'your fathers did not listen', suggests that the law had been neglected for centuries. Debt slavery was the way poor families lost their independence, and the powerful kept hold of those they had bought.

The covenant was made 'in the house that bears My Name', verse 15, so the officials went to the temple and bound themselves with a sacrifice. The calf cut in two, verse 18, belongs to a treaty ritual known well outside Israel. Genesis 15:9 to 17 records the same pattern in the covenant with Abram, and an Aramaic treaty from Sefire in Syria, from about the eighth century BC, links the cutting of a calf to a curse on the one who breaks the treaty. The point of the rite was a self-curse: may I be cut up like this animal if I break my word.

The mention of Lachish and Azekah gives a date and a mood. Letters written on pottery fragments found at Lachish come from this same period and show a garrison anxiously watching signal fires. The chapter tells us that these were the last strongholds besides Jerusalem.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs to a long biblical conversation about release. The law of Exodus 21:2 sets the principle of six years of service and freedom in the seventh, Leviticus 25:10 sets out the Jubilee, 'proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants', and Deuteronomy 15:12 to 18 explains the heart of it, that the freed slave is to be given generously, since Israel itself was redeemed from slavery. Jeremiah 34 shows the whole system tested at the one moment it was kept and then undone. The record of the Law's failure continues in Nehemiah 5, where the returned exiles again enslave their own people for debt and Nehemiah makes the nobles swear an oath and shakes out his robe as a sign of the curse, Nehemiah 5:12 and 13.

The prophets add the moral weight. Isaiah 58:6 says the fast that God chooses is 'to set the oppressed free and tear off every yoke', and Amos 2:6 condemns those who sell the needy for a pair of sandals. Jeremiah 22:3 had already demanded justice for the poor, the foreigner and the widow. On the covenant ritual, Genesis 15:17 shows God himself moving between the pieces, and Ezekiel 17:13 to 19 shows Zedekiah's broken oath to Nebuchadnezzar as a broken oath before God, 'My oath that he despised and My covenant that he broke'.

In the New Testament the word of release is taken up by Jesus. In the synagogue at Nazareth he reads Isaiah 61, 'to proclaim liberty to the captives', and says it is fulfilled in their hearing, Luke 4:18 to 21. Paul says, 'It is for freedom that Christ has set us free', Galatians 5:1, and Jesus' parable of the unforgiving servant, Matthew 18:23 to 35, repeats the shape of Jeremiah 34. A man freed from a huge debt will not release a fellow servant from a small one, and the master reverses his mercy. Hebrews 10:29 warns about those who have 'profaned the blood of the covenant', a counterpart to Jeremiah's charge that the officials 'profaned My name'.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants the hearers to understand why a city that had briefly done right was still destroyed. The chapter is the answer to an objection Jerusalem might have raised: we did repent, the king led us, we made a covenant in the temple. Verse 15 grants that this was true, 'you repented and did what pleased Me'. The point is that repentance that is withdrawn when the pressure lifts was never the real thing, and a vow made before God, then reversed for profit, is worse than no vow at all.

Jeremiah also means to show the specific sin behind the general judgment. Earlier chapters speak of idolatry and temple abuse. Here the sin is injustice done to the most vulnerable, brothers and neighbours held in debt bondage, and the passage shows that mistreating the poor is a covenant violation of the same order as worshipping another god. The word 'brother' in verses 14 and 17 is deliberate. These slaves are kin, and the officials have treated family as property.

The first hearers are also being taught about the character of the one who judges. He appeals to the exodus, not to abstract law, verse 13. The people who were redeemed from slavery are the very people who took slaves back, and the shame of that irony is the heart of the charge. The author wants the hearers to see that the law of release was never merely a rule. It was a way of remembering who had set them free.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes one historical event, a covenant in a besieged city made and broken within a short time, and it records what God said about it. It does not endorse slavery as an institution, and it does not set up the seventh year release as a programme for modern employment or debt law. The laws it quotes regulated a particular practice in a particular society, and the New Testament presses in the direction of freedom, as in Paul's plea about Onesimus, Philemon 15 and 16, and in the claim that in Christ there is neither slave nor free, Galatians 3:28.

What the chapter does prescribe, because it states the standard by which God judges, is that promises made before God must be kept even when they become costly, that the vulnerable are not to be used as conveniences, and that repentance is proved by what continues after the pressure is gone. Psalm 15:4 describes the faithful as the one 'who does not revise a costly oath', and Ecclesiastes 5:4 and 5 says it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfil. Colossians 4:1 and Ephesians 6:9 remind masters in the New Testament that they too answer to a Master in heaven. A reader should not draw from the passage that every military crisis is a divine judgment, or that Zedekiah's covenant was invalid because made under pressure. God's complaint is not that it was made in fear but that it was broken in comfort.

debates.question: Was the officials' original covenant to free their slaves a genuine act of faith, or merely a self-interested wartime tactic?

views.label: A tactical move to gain manpower for the city's defense
views.case: Some historians note the covenant may have partly aimed at freeing men for military service and reducing mouths to feed during the siege, explaining why it was so quickly reversed once the immediate danger of the Babylonian withdrawal eased.

views.label: A genuine, if short-lived, act of covenant obedience
views.case: God Himself calls it doing what pleased Me, verse 15, treating it as real repentance and real covenant-making before Him in His own house, not dismissing it as merely tactical, which makes the later betrayal all the more serious.

debates.bearing: Either reading agrees that whatever the original motive, God held the people fully accountable for the covenant they made in His name and the name they profaned in breaking it, showing that motive does not excuse a broken promise made before God.

debates.question: How can Zedekiah be promised that he will 'die in peace' when he was blinded and died a prisoner in Babylon?

views.label: The promise was conditional on surrender
views.case: Jeremiah 38:17 and 18 told Zedekiah that if he surrendered he would live and the city would not burn, and if he refused he would not escape. Zedekiah did not surrender in time. On this reading the peaceful death was offered on a condition he did not meet, as with many prophetic words that carry an implied 'if'.

views.label: Peace means a natural death with honour, not a happy life
views.case: The verse says he will not die by the sword and that spices will be burned for him as for his fathers, verses 4 and 5. 2 Kings 25:7 and Jeremiah 52:11 record that he was blinded and kept in custody until 'his dying day', which can still be a death in his bed. On this view 'peace' is a narrow promise about how he dies, and not a promise of good fortune.

debates.bearing: Neither reading disturbs the main point, that the same chapter that offers the king a mild ending also shows him presiding over the broken covenant. The prophet's word to him is real mercy and a real test, and the outcome depends on how he answers it.

debates.question: What does it mean that the officials 'passed between the pieces of the calf'?

views.label: A self-curse enacted in the ritual
views.case: The cutting of an animal and the walking between its halves, verses 18 and 19, is read as an acted oath: may I become like this animal if I break my word. This matches treaty customs known from Syria, and it explains why the LORD says he will treat the breakers 'like the calf', verse 18.

views.label: A symbol of solemn union before God
views.case: Others stress that the passing between the halves also marks a binding of the parties in the presence of the god, as in Genesis 15, where God alone walks between the pieces. On this reading the curse is implied but the main emphasis is on the seriousness of the commitment.

debates.bearing: The two readings differ in emphasis and not in outcome. In either case the ritual says that the officials had put their lives under oath, and the judgment of verses 20 to 22 shows that God took them at their word.

study.originalLanguages:
The Hebrew verb behind 'cut' in verse 18 is the ordinary verb for making a covenant, so that in Hebrew one 'cuts' a covenant, as in Genesis 15:18. The language of the rite has become the language of the treaty itself. In Jeremiah 34 the verb is pulled back to its literal sense, and the reader sees what the idiom hides: an animal killed and divided so that those who walk between the halves can say what will happen to them if they fail. The BSB uses 'cut' for the covenant and 'cut in two' for the calf to keep both senses visible. Where the Hebrew speaks of cutting a covenant, God replies by cutting the covenant breakers.

The verb 'turn' carries the drama of verses 15 and 16. In verse 15 the people 'repented' and did what pleased the LORD, and in verse 16 they 'changed your minds' and profaned his name. The BSB translates it in two ways, but the Hebrew uses the same verb of turning for both. The people turn, and then they turn back. The same movement is described in verse 11, where they 'took back' those they had freed. The verb is the basic word for repentance in the prophets, and Jeremiah uses it all the time. Here it is bent into a hinge: the same word names the turning toward God and the turning away, and the second undoes the first.

The phrase 'profaned My name', verse 16, uses a verb whose root means to make common what is holy. God's name is invoked in oaths, and Leviticus 19:12 says you must not swear falsely by his name and 'so profane the name of your God'. The officials had made their covenant in the house that bears his name, verse 15, and when they broke it they treated his name as an ordinary thing that could be used and discarded. Exodus 20:7 adds that the LORD will not leave unpunished anyone who takes his name in vain. The weight of the charge is that it goes beyond the slaves. It concerns who God is thought to be.

The family words in the passage matter. Verse 9 requires that no one hold 'his fellow Jew in bondage', and verses 14 and 17 speak of 'his brother' and 'his neighbor'. The vocabulary places the slaves in the circle of kinship and friendship, and so the re-enslavement is a betrayal of family. Verse 17 turns the key word of the chapter against the doers: God proclaims 'freedom', the same word as the proclaimed liberty of verse 8, but now it is freedom for the sword, plague and famine. The Hebrew deror is the word of Leviticus 25:10 and Isaiah 61:1, so the irony reaches back across the whole Bible. They would not give liberty, so liberty is given, and it is the liberty of being unprotected.

The word 'horror' in verse 17 translates a strong term for something that makes others shudder. The same word stands in Deuteronomy 28:25, which the BSB renders 'an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth'. The curse of the covenant that the officials had called down on themselves is now put into effect in the words of Moses. The verse about corpses becoming food for the birds and beasts, verse 20, repeats Deuteronomy 28:26 almost exactly, and so the whole sentence is a reading aloud of the covenant's own curses.

typology.type: The proclamation of liberty, Jeremiah 34:8 and 15
typology.fulfillment: Zedekiah's proclamation echoes the Jubilee of Leviticus 25:10 and is the Old Testament's picture of a release that actually frees people. Jesus announces the real thing in Luke 4:18 and 19, quoting Isaiah 61:1, and says, 'So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed', John 8:36. The correspondence is a release proclaimed to those in bondage. The escalation is that Christ's liberty reaches the bondage of sin, Romans 6:17 and 18, and cannot be taken back, because it rests on his own work and not on the goodwill of the masters. The type falls short because Judah's liberty could be revoked in a day.

typology.type: The cut calf and the passing between the pieces, Jeremiah 34:18 to 19
typology.fulfillment: The ritual says that a covenant is made in death. Hebrews 9:18 to 22 says the first covenant 'was not put into effect without blood' and that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. In Genesis 15:17 God himself passes between the pieces, taking the oath on himself, and in Jeremiah 34 the people pass between them and the curse falls on them. In Christ the curse falls on God's own Son, who 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us', Galatians 3:13, and he says, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood', Luke 22:20. The type is limited because an animal's death cannot absorb a covenant curse, but the one who dies in the covenant here is the covenant maker.

typology.type: The release grounded in the exodus, Jeremiah 34:13 to 14
typology.fulfillment: God says he brought them 'out of the house of slavery' and that this is the reason they must free their own. The New Testament takes the same logic of redeemed people who free others. Hebrews 2:14 and 15 says Christ came to 'free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death', and Matthew 18:23 to 35 shows the redeemed servant who will not release a fellow servant. The correspondence is that the freed are obliged to free. The type shows its limit in that Israel's exodus freed a nation from Egypt, whereas Christ frees people from sin and death.

typology.type: A covenant broken in the house that bears God's name, Jeremiah 34:15 to 16
typology.fulfillment: The officials treated a solemn promise in the temple as disposable. Hebrews 10:29 says a person who has 'trampled on the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant that sanctified him, and insulted the Spirit of grace' deserves worse punishment than one who broke the law of Moses. This is a warning and not a prediction, and it falls short as a type because it does not show Christ himself. It does show that the seriousness of the covenant increases as the covenant becomes greater.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ by contrast and by the thing it lacks. It describes a freedom proclaimed and withdrawn, a covenant made and broken, and a judgment that falls on the covenant breakers. Each of these is met by Christ in a way that changes the outcome. Where Zedekiah's liberty was announced by a king and revoked by his officials, Jesus stands up in Nazareth and reads from Isaiah, 'He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives... to release the oppressed', Luke 4:18, and the release is not revoked. John 8:34 to 36 sets the principle: everyone who sins is a slave to sin, but a son belongs to the family forever, and 'if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed'. The distinction between a slave and a son is the whole difference between Zedekiah's covenant and Christ's. A slave can be sold again, and a son cannot be dispossessed.

The cut calf points to what the covenant cost. The officials passed between the halves and called a curse on themselves, and the curse arrived within a few years. At the cross, the curse that belongs to covenant breakers fell on the one who had never broken a covenant, Galatians 3:13. The picture of Genesis 15 is also important. In that chapter only God passes between the pieces, in the form of a smoking firepot and a flaming torch, while Abram sleeps. The covenant of grace is held by God's own oath. Hebrews 6:13 and 17 develops this idea. In Jeremiah 34 the humans take the oath and fail, and in Christ God takes the oath on himself. This is why the new covenant cannot be broken from God's side, and why Jesus can say of the cup that it is the new covenant in his blood.

There is a further Christlike pattern that should be named with care. The slaves of Jeremiah 34 are the weak, handed from one master to another by people in power. Jesus describes his own coming in exactly these terms: 'the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many', Matthew 20:28. The one who has the right to be master takes the place of the slave, and Philippians 2:7 says that he took 'the form of a servant'. The chapter's moral demand that the powerful release the poor is met in a person who gave up power to release them.

The chapter also prepares the hearer for the gospel's warning. Matthew 18 and Jeremiah 34 teach the same truth, that those who receive mercy must show it. James 2:13 says that judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Believers are not saved by their mercy, but a life that refuses to forgive those who owe it little shows that the gift has not been understood. The chapter ends in judgment, and the cross is where that judgment is borne for those who trust him.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is first of all the one who frees. When he states his case against Judah he does not begin with a list of rules. He begins with himself, 'I made a covenant with your forefathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery', verse 13. His identity is bound up with the liberation of slaves, and so the re-enslavement of those freed in his name is an offence against his character. In Leviticus 25:55 the same claim is made in a single sentence, 'They are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt', and the people who had been brought out cannot lawfully be possessed by someone else.

He is also patient and exact. He notes that the people 'repented and did what pleased Me', verse 15, and he does not dismiss it. God's justice does not ignore good, and his judgment does not come on a whim. Verse 14 reminds the hearers that their fathers did not listen, and verses 17 to 22 spell out a sentence that matches the offence word for word. The God of the chapter is not arbitrary, and he is not a God to be outbargained. He takes covenant seriously because he is a covenant keeper himself.

The chapter also shows a God who guards his own name. Verse 16 says that the officials 'profaned My name'. It matters to God what is done in his name, since he has placed himself in the world through his people. When people use his name to swear and then break their oath, the credibility of the one named is at stake before the nations, which is what Paul says in Romans 2:24, 'God's name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you'. The jealousy for his name is not vanity. It is concern that the true God not be misrepresented.

There is real tenderness in verses 4 and 5. In a chapter of judgment he promises the king a peaceful death and a mourning crowd, and he adds, 'For I Myself have spoken this word'. That emphasis shows that even in the siege God speaks personally to those who rule, and that his warnings are mingled with kindness. Judgment is not his only mode. In Ezekiel 33:11 he says he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.

For worship this means we praise a God who is the liberator and the judge of liberators who betray. He is faithful when we are not, and he will not be mocked by promises made in his house. We are taught to guard our word, to treat the weak as kin, and to trust that his own mercy, shown in the exodus and the cross, is more solid than any pledge we make.

crossReferences.note: The law of the seventh year says that a Hebrew servant serves six years and goes free in the seventh without paying anything. Jeremiah 34:14 cites this as the covenant the fathers did not obey, and it shows that the release that the officials briefly kept had stood in the law since Sinai.

The fuller form of the release law, with its demand that the freed servant be sent off generously and its reason: remember that you were slaves in Egypt and the LORD redeemed you. This is the theology behind the exodus appeal of Jeremiah 34:13, and it explains why re-enslaving a brother is a forgetting of grace.

The Jubilee command to 'proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants' is the source of the word deror in Jeremiah 34. The echo shows that Zedekiah's proclamation meant to honour this ancient ideal, and that its reversal mocks the very law that gave the word.

The covenant with Abram, in which animals are divided and God alone passes between the pieces as a smoking firepot and a flaming torch. This is the background to the calf of Jeremiah 34:18 and shows what the rite means, and in Genesis the oath is taken by God, whereas in Jeremiah the oath is taken by the people.

Ezekiel describes the same king breaking his covenant with Babylon and says God will bring his broken oath down on his head. It sets Zedekiah's oath to Nebuchadnezzar beside the covenant of Jeremiah 34, and shows that the king's habit of breaking oaths is the pattern of the whole chapter.

The Babylonian army withdraws when Pharaoh's army sets out from Egypt. This is the lull that explains the timing of the reversal in 34:11 and the phrase 'that had withdrawn from you' in 34:21, and it shows how quickly a changed circumstance became an excuse to change a promise.

Generations later the people again enslave their own for debt, and Nehemiah shakes out his robe in an acted curse on those who break the promise. The scene replays Jeremiah 34 with a better ending: the nobles restore what they took and keep their oath.

The anointed one comes to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners. Jesus quotes it in Nazareth, and so the word that Judah's officials proclaimed and cancelled returns in the mouth of the one who will not cancel it.

The parable of the servant forgiven a vast debt who throttles a fellow servant over a small one. It has the shape of Jeremiah 34, a release received and not extended, and it ends in the same way, with the master reversing his mercy.

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. The cut calf of Jeremiah 34 pictures the curse that falls on covenant breakers, and Galatians shows who bore it for those who trust him.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a God who creates a people in his image to live freely in his presence, and the fall puts humanity under a rule of sin and death. The exodus is the great early act of redemption, when God hears the cry of slaves and brings them out of Egypt so that they will be his people and serve him, not Pharaoh. The law of release in Jeremiah 34 is the exodus kept alive in the ordinary life of the nation: whenever an Israelite let a debtor go, he was rehearsing the story of how he himself had been let go.

What this chapter answers from before is the question whether Israel has really been changed by redemption. The answer is no. Deuteronomy 15 had said that Israel must remember and release, and the nation had forgotten. The calf that is cut in two is the old covenant's own warning of what happens to a people who say yes to God and then act as though they had said no. The verdict of exile is the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28 being carried out, and Jeremiah 34 shows the specific sin that tipped the scales.

What it sets up is the need for a deeper release. Jeremiah 31:31 to 34 promises a new covenant in which God's law is written within, so that obedience is not a matter of a covenant that people can break. Isaiah 61 promises an anointed one who will proclaim liberty to the captives, and the Gospels announce that he has come. Jesus takes the slave's place, bears the curse of the covenant breakers, and makes a covenant that is sealed in his own blood. The freedom he proclaims is not revoked, because it does not depend on the faithfulness of those who receive it.

The end of the story is a people freed for good. Revelation 21 describes a city where there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, and Romans 8 says that creation itself will be freed from its bondage. In that day nobody takes anybody back. The freed live as sons in the household, and the proclamation of liberty sounded in Jerusalem and cancelled by its officials sounds for the last time and is never recalled. Until then, the church lives between Jeremiah 34 and Revelation 21, called to extend the liberty it has received, to keep the promises it has made, and to remember who brought it out of the house of slavery.

quiz.q: What does God tell Zedekiah about his own fate in verses 4 to 5?

options.text: He will not die by the sword but will die in peace, with proper mourning rites, even though the city will fall.
options.note: Verses 4 to 5 give this specific, somewhat merciful promise even amid the announcement of the city's fall.

options.text: He will escape Babylon entirely and remain king.
options.note: The text explicitly says he will be captured and taken to Babylon, not that he escapes.

options.text: He will die by the sword like his officials.
options.note: God specifically promises he will not die by the sword but will die in peace.

options.text: He will be restored to the throne after a brief exile.
options.note: The text promises his death in Babylon, not a restoration to Judah's throne.

quiz.q: What covenant does Zedekiah lead the people to make in verses 8 to 10?

options.text: To free every Hebrew slave, male and female, so that no one holds a fellow Jew in bondage.
options.note: Verses 8 to 9 specify this covenant, obeying the long-neglected sabbatical release law.

options.text: To surrender the city immediately to Babylon.
options.note: The covenant concerns freeing Hebrew slaves, not military surrender.

options.text: To free only male slaves, keeping female slaves in bondage.
options.note: The covenant explicitly includes both male and female slaves.

options.text: To raise taxes to fund the city's defense.
options.note: The covenant concerns releasing slaves, not a taxation measure.

quiz.q: What do the officials do after initially freeing their slaves, verse 11?

options.text: They changed their minds and forced the freed men and women back into slavery.
options.note: Verse 11 explicitly describes this reversal, re-enslaving those they had just freed.

options.text: They freed even more slaves than the covenant required.
options.note: The text describes the opposite, a reversal and re-enslavement, not further generosity.

options.text: They kept their covenant faithfully throughout the siege.
options.note: The whole point of God's rebuke in verses 12 to 16 is that they broke this covenant.

options.text: They freed the slaves but only after the city had fallen.
options.note: The freeing and subsequent re-enslaving both occurred before the final judgment described in this chapter.

quiz.q: What judgment does God pronounce because of this broken covenant, verses 17 to 20?

options.text: He proclaims freedom for them instead, freedom to fall by sword, famine, and plague, and treats the covenant breakers like the calf they cut in two.
options.note: Verses 17 to 18 give this specific, ironic judgment answering their broken promise of freedom.

options.text: He forgives them without any consequence since they had once obeyed.
options.note: The text describes severe judgment, not forgiveness without consequence.

options.text: He judges only the slaves who were re-enslaved, not the officials who broke the covenant.
options.note: The judgment falls specifically on the officials, priests, and people who broke the covenant, not on the slaves.

options.text: He delays judgment indefinitely with no specific consequence named.
options.note: Verses 17 to 20 name specific, severe consequences: sword, plague, famine, and death by their enemies.

quiz.q: How does the liberty, deror, proclaimed and betrayed in this chapter anticipate the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates by contrast the true liberty Christ proclaims to captives in Luke 4:18-19, a release He never revokes.
options.note: Jesus explicitly reads and applies Isaiah's promise of liberty to captives to His own ministry, in deliberate contrast to any liberty later withdrawn.

options.text: There is no meaningful connection between this chapter and the New Testament.
options.note: The recurring Hebrew word deror links directly to Isaiah 61:1 and Christ's own reading of it in Luke 4:18-19.

options.text: It anticipates only future Roman laws about slavery.
options.note: The connection drawn is theological, to Christ's proclaimed and unrevoked liberty, not to Roman civil law.

options.text: It anticipates a liberty that Christ also later revokes.
options.note: The contrast is precisely that Christ's proclaimed liberty, unlike Judah's officials, is never revoked.

questions: Judah's officials made a genuine covenant of freedom and then reversed it once the danger passed. Where have you made a promise to God or to someone else that you have quietly taken back once it became inconvenient?

God took special notice of how His people treated the most vulnerable among them, those in bondage. Who are the vulnerable people in your life or community whose freedom and dignity you might be overlooking?

God reminded the people that He Himself had first freed them from slavery in Egypt, giving weight to what they owed each other. How does remembering what Christ has freed you from shape how you treat others?
The covenant they broke was made specifically before God, in His own house. Is there a promise you have made before God that needs to be kept rather than quietly abandoned?

Christ proclaims a liberty He never revokes, unlike the officials in this chapter. Where do you need to trust that the freedom Christ has given you is permanent and not conditional on your own performance?

translationNotes.note: The burning of spices for a deceased king was a customary royal funeral honor, not a form of cremation; God's promise that this rite would be performed for Zedekiah, despite his coming captivity, is itself a real mercy amid judgment.

The sabbatical release law being invoked here, Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12, had apparently gone unpracticed for generations, showing that Judah's covenant unfaithfulness in this area long predated the crisis of the siege.

The ritual of cutting a calf in two and walking between the pieces, also seen in Genesis 15:9-17, symbolized the fate the covenant maker called down on himself if he broke the covenant's terms, making God's judgment here a direct application of the officials' own ceremony against themselves.
